newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen on defensive in Europe as G3 plans mulled.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen on defensive in Europe as G3 plans mulled.

text.p: The wind was taken from dollar/yen's sails on Wednesday in Europe after a news report said Japan, the U.S. and Germany were planning to sell dollars for yen and persuaded nervous traders to cut dollar positions.

The U.S. currency lost almost one yen after the report which, citing an international monetary source, said the so-called Group of Three was exploring the possibility of a joint effort to sell dollars for yen to prevent further yen weakness.
"There hasn't been that much activity today but talk of intervention was enough to encourage a wave of profit-taking," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.

At 1510 GMT, the dollar was trading at 125.00/10 yen down from 124.45/55 late Tuesday but off the intraday low at 124.60. The dollar/yen rate has risen more than 10 percent this year to a 56-month high at 127.46 on May 1.
Against the mark, the dollar was 1.7210/15 compared with 1.72.24/29 late Tuesday.
Analysts said the intervention concern stems more from yen weakness than mark weakness, leaving the mark/yen cross vulnerable in the process.
"Whatever the view on dollar/yen, it's very difficult to believe Germany would want to rally the mark," said Hawkins.

The report on intervention, carried by Japan's Kyodo news agency, was fuelled later after a Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said Japan could use its $220 billion worth of external reserves promptly if needed.

Yet there was no indication outside Japan that intervention was being discussed. A Bundesbank spokeswoman declined to comment on the Kyodo report, saying Germany stood by the G7 statement from Washington last month.
The April G7 statement called for exchange rates to reflect fundamentals and said excess volatility was undesireable.
Recent Bundesbank comments reflects this, analysts said.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said late Tuesday the central bank could not welcome further dollar gains but a spokesman later stressed that Welteke was happy with current levels and did not have a specific target.
"The idea of some new G3 agreement seems a bit ridiculous," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.

"There are long-standing arrangements in place about this sort of international coordination and, in any event, it really is just up to Japan at the moment," he said. "It's not as if they don't have the ammunition themselves."
There was no comment on the dollar today from the U.S.

U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Lawrence Summers declined to comment on the Kyodo report but confirmed that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had cut short a trip to Mexico to catch up with regular Treasury business.
"The Rubin story raised a few eyebrows but is more likely to be something to do with the balanced budget negotiations than anything to do with the dollar," said a trader at a UK bank.

News of a rise in the Japanese trade surplus to 352.67 billion yen in the first 20 days of April from 59.06 billion in the same period last year also weighed on dollar/yen but the trade data is seen as erratic lately, analysts said.
"The trade data has been extremely choppy of late and there's not such an obvious trend," said Von Maydell at UBS.
The latest U.S. economic data later in the day helped the dollar recover from lows, traders said. However, economists said the numbers were a bit too dated to have a lasting effect.
First-quarter unit labour costs rose 2.7 percent, up from 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and well above the 1.0 percent growth forecast.
Traders are now awaiting the release of the Federal Reserve's key economic assessment, the Beige Book, at 1800 GMT.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
